shortSummary: Majestic dipterocarp timber giant dominating Bangladesh's Madhupur and Bhawal Bhawal-Terrace deciduous forests with winged five-sepalled samaras and fragrant dammar resin.
leadOverview: Shorea robusta, revered across South Asia as Sal and regionally in central Bangladesh as Gojari, is one of the most ecologically dominant broadleaf timber trees of the Indian subcontinent. Anchoring the red lateritic Pleistocene terraces of Madhupur and Bhawal, this towering semi-deciduous dipterocarp yields exceptionally durable heartwood, aromatic dammar resin, and winged shuttlecock-like fruits.

sections.title: Morphological Description
sections.subtitle: Cylindrical fissured boles, glossy ovate leaves, cream panicles, and winged samaras
sections.summary: Canopy form, leathery deciduous-flush foliage, creamy yellow panicles, and winged Dipterocarpaceae fruits.
paragraphs: Shorea robusta grows into a straight-boled forest giant reaching 25 to 50 metres in height with a clean cylindrical trunk clad in thick, dark greyish-brown longitudinally furrowed bark up to 5 centimetres deep—an adaptation shielding cambial tissue against dry-season ground fires. Under dense woodland shade, natural self-pruning produces long knot-free timber stems.

Leaves are simple, alternate, broadly ovate-oblong (10–25 cm long) with cordate bases, 12 to 15 pairs of prominent parallel lateral veins, and reddish young flushes in spring. In Boshonto, drooping panicles of creamy-yellow fragrant flowers give way within 10 to 12 weeks to nut-like ovoid fruits crowned by three enlarged and two shorter papery calyx wings.

sections.title: Taxonomy & Botanical Classification
sections.subtitle: Malvales dipterocarp lineage and recalcitrant-seed physiology
sections.summary: Taxonomic position within Dipterocarpaceae named for its characteristic winged calyx fruits.
paragraphs: Placed in the order Malvales and family Dipterocarpaceae—named from Greek 'di-' (two) and 'pteron' (wing) after its winged fruiting calyx—Shorea robusta represents the westernmost gregarious dipterocarp species spanning the Indo-Gangetic piedmont. Karl Friedrich Gaertner published the binomial in 1805.

Unlike orthodox dryland seeds, Sal nuts are strictly recalcitrant: they contain high moisture at dispersal and lose germination viability within 10 to 14 days if dried, synchronizing fruit fall precisely with early monsoon cloudbursts.

sections.title: Natural Habitat & Global Distribution
sections.subtitle: Madhupur Tract, Bhawal National Park, and Himalayan Terai foothills
sections.summary: Moist-deciduous red-clay terrace forests across Bangladesh, northern India, and Nepal.
paragraphs: Shorea robusta forms pure gregarious stands across well-drained Pleistocene lateritic uplands and sub-Himalayan Terai belts from Himachal Pradesh and Nepal across Assam to central and northern Bangladesh. It thrives in annual rainfall regimes of 1,000 to 2,500 millimetres on acidic red clay-loam (pH 5.0–6.5), avoiding waterlogged floodplains.

In Bangladesh, remnant Sal (Gojari) forests define the Madhupur Tract (Tangail and Mymensingh), Bhawal National Park (Gazipur), and isolated northern patches in Dinajpur and Rangpur, sheltering Garo indigenous agroforestry communities and rare woodland wildlife.

sections.title: Ecological Role & Pollinator Interactions
sections.subtitle: Thrips pollination, ectomycorrhizal networks, and coppice regeneration
sections.summary: Wind-assisted thrips pollination, soil fungal symbiosis, and wildlife habitat value.
paragraphs: Sal blossoms release a sweet musky scent attracting tiny thrips, honeybees, and solitary beetles that cross-pollinate neighboring trees amidst open spring winds. Beneath the forest floor, Sal roots form vital ectomycorrhizal symbioses with Russula and Amanita basidiomycete mushrooms that unlock scarce phosphorus from weathered red clay.

Historically renowned for extraordinary coppice vigor, felled stumps sprout multiple vigorous shoots from underground root collars, supporting capped langurs, woodpeckers, and wild junglefowl across Madhupur.

sections.title: Economic, Culinary & Cultural Importance
sections.subtitle: Termite-resistant timber, dhuna incense, and stitched eco-plates
sections.summary: Heavy structural hardwood, sacred resin incense, sal-butter seed fat, and sustainable leaf ware.
paragraphs: Sal ranks among South Asia's premier structural hardwoods—exceptionally dense, resin-impregnated, and naturally resistant to termites and rot—traditionally milled into bridge pilings, railway sleepers, boat keels, and heavy door frames. Extracted oleoresin ('dhuna' or sal dammar) serves as aromatic ceremonial incense and boat-caulking pitch.

Across rural eastern India and Bangladesh, fallen tough Sal leaves are stitched with bamboo slivers into sturdy biodegradable bowls and platters ('sal pata thala'), while seed kernels yield pale green sal butter used in soapmaking and confectionery.

sections.title: Traditional & Scientific Medicinal Properties
sections.subtitle: Resin triterpenoids, astringent bark tannins, and dermal balms
sections.summary: Antimicrobial sal dammar ointments and tannin-rich bark decoctions in folk pharmacology.
paragraphs: In Ayurveda (known as 'Shala') and Unani practice, powdered white Sal resin (Ral) is warmed with sesame oil or ghee to formulate soothing topical balms for skin abrasions, cracked heels, and minor burns. Phytochemical assays identify ursolic acid, asiatic acid, and alpha-amyrin triterpenoids with documented antibacterial and wound-healing properties.
Stem bark extracts are rich in condensed tannins and bergenin, traditionally prepared as astringent gargles and gastrointestinal tonics.
sections.safetyNote: Crude Sal resin (dhuna) should only be used topically or as external fumigation incense unless formulated by a qualified practitioner; resinous smoke may irritate asthma-prone airways.

sections.title: Comprehensive Cultivation & Care Guide
sections.subtitle: Immediate fresh-seed sowing, ectomycorrhizal soil inoculation, and deep taproots
sections.summary: Raising Shorea robusta from short-lived winged seeds on acidic well-drained loam.
paragraphs: Because Sal seeds lose viability rapidly after hitting the ground in late Grishmo (May–June), collect freshly fallen green-winged nuts and sow them immediately half-buried in deep nursery polybags filled with acidic red loam (pH 5.0–6.5) blended with topsoil from a healthy Sal woodland to transfer beneficial mycorrhizal fungi.

Avoid bare-root transplanting, as seedlings form a long sensitive taproot early; plant out ball-of-earth saplings at monsoon onset with 3-to-4-metre spacing, shielding young shoots from browsing livestock and dry-season grass fires during the first three years.

sections.title: Annual Phenology & Six-Season Rhythms
sections.subtitle: Flowering, fruiting, vegetative flush, and Shororitu synchrony
sections.summary: Seasonal cadence across Bengal's six-season cycle (Spring (বসন্ত), Summer (গ্রীষ্ম)).
paragraphs: Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) aligns its vegetative flushes, anthesis, and fruit maturation tightly with Bengal's Shororitu photoperiod and monsoon moisture transitions, showing peak biological activity during Spring (বসন্ত), Summer (গ্রীষ্ম).

Spring (বসন্ত): Sheds weathered winter foliage briefly before bursting into fragrant creamy-yellow panicles and ruby leaf flushes. Summer (গ্রীষ্ম): Five-winged Dipterocarpaceae samaras spin onto Madhupur red clay for immediate pre-monsoon germination.

sections.title: Seed Germination Biology & Propagation
sections.subtitle: Dormancy regulation, nursery media, and clonal propagation
sections.summary: Reproductive biology and reliable seed or vegetative propagation techniques for Sal Tree.
paragraphs: Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) combines sexual seed propagation—useful for raising sturdy heterozygous rootstocks—with elite clonal techniques such as veneer grafting, air layering (gootee), and semi-hardwood stem cuttings. Fresh recalcitrant or semi-orthodox seeds typically germinate within 14 to 35 days when depulped and sown in warm organic loam.
Clonal orchards standardize crown architecture, early precocity, and uniform biochemical profiles across generations within Dipterocarpaceae.

subblocks.heading: Nursery Seed Protocol
subblocks.text: Depulped seed sown cleanly in 2:1 loam-compost media; high viability when fresh.

subblocks.heading: Clonal Method
subblocks.text: Approach/veneer grafting or monsoon air-layering onto vigorous local rootstocks.

sections.title: Pathology Defense, Vectors & Organic IPM
sections.subtitle: Phytoalexin resilience, fungal prophylaxis, and predator guilds
sections.summary: Biochemical defense mechanisms and low-impact organic IPM guidelines for Shorea robusta.
paragraphs: In humid South Asian and tropical growing belts, Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) relies on secondary terpenoid resins, foliar trichomes, and phytoalexin phenolics as front-line biochemical deterrence against herbivores and opportunistic pathogens. Prolonged monsoon waterlogging or stagnant canopy humidity can nonetheless encourage anthracnose (Colletotrichum spp.), powdery mildew, leaf-spot fungi, or root-zone Pythium.

Organic Integrated Pest Management (IPM) prioritizes preventive airflow pruning, Trichoderma-enriched compost amendments around feeder roots, and targeted cold-pressed Azadirachta indica (neem) oil sprays at dusk to suppress sap-sucking aphids, scale insects, and mealybugs without harming native pollinators.

subblocks.heading: Fungal Management
subblocks.text: Prevent overhead foliar wetness at dusk; maintain canopy aeration and copper/Trichoderma prophylaxis.

subblocks.heading: Organic Pest Control
subblocks.text: Neem kernel emulsion (3–5 ml/L) plus conservation of hoverfly and ladybird predator guilds.

sections.title: Conservation Standing & Climate Resilience
sections.subtitle: Population security, agroforestry corridors, and stress tolerance
sections.summary: Biogeographic conservation standing and climate adaptation traits of Sal Tree.
paragraphs: Across its native and naturalized distribution (South Asia (Sub-Himalayan & Madhupur-Bhawal Belts)), Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) demonstrates strong ecological plasticity across alluvial floodplains, homestead agroforestry plots, and urban biodiversity corridors. While cultivated stands remain broadly secure, landrace genetic erosion, coastal salinity shifts, and wetland drainage threaten wild ecotypes and heritage regional varieties.

Long-term resilience depends on decentralized in-situ homestead stewardship, wetland buffer conservation, and botanical garden germplasm collections preserving drought-, flood-, and salinity-tolerant alleles amid shifting monsoon regimes.

subblocks.text: Adapted to South Asia (Sub-Himalayan & Madhupur-Bhawal Belts) thermal oscillations and seasonal hydrological extremes.

sections.title: Horticultural Spacing, Pruning & Telemetry
sections.subtitle: Plot geometry, canopy shaping, and calibrated soil-climate meters
sections.summary: Calibrated horticultural parameters: pH 5.0 – 6.5, Full Sun / Emergent Canopy, and structural spacing guidance.
paragraphs: Optimal managed cultivation of Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) calibrates root-zone chemistry around pH 5.0 – 6.5 inside well-drained lateritic red loam. Providing adequate crown spacing prevents humidity buildup and lets lower shoots capture uniform irradiance across full sun / emergent canopy.

Light corrective pruning immediately after main flowering or harvest periods redirects assimilates into healthy vegetative framework, while moisture scheduling (moderate seasonal monsoon) stabilizes root turgor without inducing hypoxia.

sections.title: Evolutionary Genetics & Adaptive Phylogeny
sections.subtitle: Malvales clade divergence and Dipterocarpaceae genomic traits
sections.summary: Phylogenetic placement of genus Shorea within order Malvales (Eudicot (Malvids)).
paragraphs: Modern molecular phylogenetics (APG IV) places Shorea robusta inside family Dipterocarpaceae (ডিপ্টেরোকার্পাসি (শাল-গর্জন গোত্র)), order Malvales, clade Eudicot (Malvids). Resin-bearing tropical hardwood giants anchoring South and Southeast Asian broadleaf forests, instantly recognizable by shuttlecock-like winged fruiting calyces.

Within genus Shorea, specialized morphological adaptations—such as woody ovoid nuts crowned with two to five persistent papery calyx wings—reflect co-evolutionary specialization with regional pollinator guilds and abiotic habitat filters.

sections.title: Field Identification Key & Diagnostic Checks
sections.subtitle: Macro-morphological verification against look-alike taxa
sections.summary: Rapid field-sheet checklist for confirming Shorea robusta (Shal / Gojari (শাল / গজারী)).
paragraphs: Field verification of Sal Tree (Shorea robusta) rests on recognizing key Dipterocarpaceae family markers: Woody ovoid nuts crowned with two to five persistent papery calyx wings; Deeply fissured fire-hardy bark containing aromatic dammar oleoresins; Ectomycorrhizal root symbiosis supporting gregarious terrace stands. Inspecting fresh leaf arrangement, stem surface texture, and reproductive architecture together eliminates confusion with sympatric congeners.

Fire-Hardy Bark & Bole: Deeply fissured charcoal-brown bark packed with resin canals yielding pale aromatic Sal dammar (dhuna). Coriaceous Leaf Blades: Tough, leathery ovate foliage shed briefly between Phalgun and Chaitra before flushing ruby-copper. Creamy Raceme Panicles: Fragrant five-petalled cream blossoms densely clustered along defoliated spring twigs. Winged Dipterocarp Samaras: Helicopter-like five-winged fruits spinning smoothly in pre-monsoon gusts for rapid immediate germination.
